catalog_quote: [Kashoki & Mann 1978, p. 70] In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed ... In some languages, hovvever, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syilable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. Hovvever, it must be remembered that that is also the syilable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, vvhich is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vovvel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vovvels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish vvords from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. ... [pp. 63-64] in ali the languages of the Eastern Province (including Nyanja) ... the penultimate syllable, i.e. the syllable before the final one, of a word is always lengthened. ... [S…

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both Kashoki & Mann 1978 passages (pp. 63-64 penult lengthening in all Eastern Province languages; p. 70 syllables evenly stressed, penult force = lengthening, stress non-distinctive, every syllable carries tone) and the Ranger 1928 p. vii/fn. 5 passages are verbatim at the stated locators in the held text files, and Simango 2006 (held PDF) independently states for Nsenga itself that penult lengthening is non-phonemic and that H/L/Falling tone is lexical and grammatical, with no stress or accent anywhere in the sketch. Hyman 2013 (fetched sources now, open) lists N41 Nsenga among penultimate-lengthening languages, consistent.
